Palantir Technologies Inc. PLTR continues to demonstrate exceptional operating momentum, with its Rule of 40 score reaching 158% in the third quarter of 2026 compared with 81% in the fourth quarter of 2024. The sustained improvement highlights the company's ability to accelerate revenue growth while strengthening profitability, reinforcing its competitive positioning in the artificial intelligence (AI) software market.

The Rule of 40 combines revenue growth and adjusted operating margin to assess the balance between expansion and profitability. Palantir's performance substantially exceeds the conventional 40% benchmark, underscoring its operating strength.

PLTR's Accelerating Revenue Growth Strengthens Its Score

Palantir's Rule of 40 improved from 145% in the first quarter of 2026 to 155% in the second quarter and 158% in the third. The latest reading reflects 96% year-over-year revenue growth and a 62% adjusted operating margin.

The company's expanding Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) adoption is supporting this momentum. U.S. commercial revenues surged 148% year over year to $984 million, reflecting growing enterprise demand for AI-driven operational capabilities.

Meanwhile, U.S. government revenues increased 96%, demonstrating strong demand across public-sector customers. This diversified growth provides additional support for sustaining the company's elevated performance.

Improving Profitability Reinforces PLTR's Growth Prospects

Palantir's expanding operating leverage is another important contributor to its Rule of 40 performance. Adjusted operating income reached $1.43 billion, while adjusted free cash flow totaled $1.22 billion, representing a 53% margin.

Management's raised full-year revenue guidance of $8.530-$8.534 billion further strengthens confidence in continued business expansion.

However, sustaining such exceptional growth and profitability simultaneously could become increasingly challenging as the revenue base expands. Elevated investor expectations also leave limited room for operational disappointments.

Nevertheless, Palantir's accelerating enterprise adoption, substantial operating margins and expanding cash generation suggest that its Rule of 40 performance remains a compelling indicator of underlying business strength.

How Do PLTR's Industry Peers Compare?

Snowflake SNOW and Datadog DDOG are two U.S.-listed software companies benefiting from enterprise AI adoption. Snowflake reported 35% revenue growth in its second quarter of fiscal 2027, supported by increasing demand for its AI Data Cloud offerings. Snowflake continues to expand its enterprise relationships through broader data analytics and AI capabilities.

S&P requires IPOs to trade 12 months before index consideration, so Anthropic can't enter S&P 500 funds until late 2027 at the earliest.

Anthropic must also post positive GAAP profits for the latest quarter and trailing four quarters, but its filing shows a recent net loss.

Consider a hypothetical 61-year-old with $1 million in an S&P 500 index fund inside his 401(k). He reads that Anthropic filed for an IPO on October 26. He assumes the company behind Claude will show up in his account within weeks of its debut. Retirees have been wondering for months how SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI would affect their retirement accounts.

24/7 Wall St.

Anthropic has applied to list its Class A shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, with trading expected to begin November 19. His S&P 500 fund won't buy the stock on day one, and it could be years before it does.

A 12-Month Clock Starts at the Opening Bell

Under S&P's rules, IPOs "should be traded on an eligible exchange for at least 12 months before being considered for addition to an index." If Anthropic lists in late November, the index committee can't consider it until late 2027 at the earliest.

That rule almost changed. On April 30, 2026, S&P Dow Jones Indices asked for feedback on cutting the waiting period to six months from 12 months for megacap companies. On June 4, 2026, the committee decided against it, concluding that exceptions "should not be granted solely based on market capitalization."

title: Obscure Defense Tech Company Sees 1,550% Revenue Jump
detail:
Obscure Defense Tech Company Sees 1,550% Revenue Jump
Photo via Juliane Sonntag/IMAGO//Newscom

Trading disclosure

Concerned about an AI bubble? Sign up for The Daily Upside for smart and actionable market news, built for investors.

A lot can change in a year, just usually not this much.

On Thursday, little-known defense tech company Ondas reported third-quarter revenue of $167 million, marking a stunning year-over-year increase of more than 1,550%, or a 16.5-fold jump for the less math inclined. That's impressive, just not to Wall Street. Shares of the company sank 7% on Thursday, thanks to a quarterly $0.11 earnings per share loss that came in larger than expectations. Consider the report a sign of the major growth — and correlated major expectations — for the next generation of defense firms.

Sign up for The Daily Upside at no cost for premium analysis on all your favorite stocks.

READ ALSO: When Bad News Is Good News: Nvidia Rival Led by Jensen Huang's Cousin Rallies Amid Ex-CEO's 'Spy Soap Opera' and Kraft Heinz Wants to Win Back the Modern Eater

FIFA's Top Defender

The growth was not entirely organic. The company, primarily a maker of autonomous drones, has been on an aggressive M&A shopping spree, including six key acquisitions in the most recent quarter mostly across the drone and autonomous weapons space. A year ago, Ondas acquired counter-drone systems company Sentrycs, whose tech was employed at many World Cup host stadiums this summer. However, pro forma organic revenue, which includes portfolio companies' preacquisition sales in the prior period, still grew 64% year over year in the third quarter.

Ondas expects the rapid growth will continue:

Full-year revenue is now expected to reach "at least" $550 million, which was the high end of its previous forecast range. For next year, Ondas said it is setting an initial revenue target of $1.1 billion. Its order book, meanwhile, surged 36% from the prior quarter to $835 million.

Still, gross margins dropped to 21% from 43% a quarter prior; total losses reached $64 million, way up from just $7 million a year ago. On the bright side, companywide adjusted EBITDA profitability is now expected to arrive in next year's third quarter, Ondas said, one quarter earlier than it previously estimated.

Alex Karp Fishing: The most significant recent development for Ondas may just be a new partnership with Palantir. In October, the two firms announced Regna AI, a standalone company "initially wholly owned by Ondas" and "powered by Palantir" that aims to help customers "deploy mission-specialized fine-tuned AI models within their own sovereign environments," the two firms said in a statement.
